items.title: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
items.desc: We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.

items.title: Device that measures strawberry skin's strength will aid breeders
items.desc: Resilient strawberry varieties will be more easily identifiable thanks to a tool developed by University of Queensland engineering students. The prototype measures the strength of strawberry skin, a key breeding consideration for the Australian Strawberry Breeding Program at Queensland's Department of Primary Industries.

items.title: Quantum software matches classical benchmark for a molecular interaction
items.desc: Predicting how molecules interact is central to drug discovery: it offers important information about how a new drug might work in the human body, the side effects it can cause and more. Computationally modeling these interactions can reduce the need for lengthy and expensive lab work, but some interactions still remain beyond the reach of classical computers.

items.title: The call of the seamount: Two new armored tardigrades described in the Atlantic
items.desc: An international team led by researchers from Senckenberg am Meer in Wilhelmshaven has described two new species of marine tardigrades. The tiny marine organisms were discovered in the sediment of the Senghor Seamount off the coast of Cape Verde. According to the researchers, the discovery underscores the role of undersea mountains as oases of biodiversity. The study, which includes comprehensive taxonomic descriptions of the new species, has been published in the journal "ZooKeys."

items.title: Broadening the role of RNA: A messenger, a mediator and now a condensate coordinator
items.desc: New research about condensates—cellular compartments that act as hubs for facilitating biological reactions—continues to reveal novel insights into how cells function. Among those continuing to push the field forward are members of the Marine Biological Laboratory's condensate consortium, including Amy Gladfelter, a professor at Duke University and current co-director of the MBL physiology course, and former MBL physiology course student and past MBL Whitman fellow Dragomir Milovanovic, a professor at the Charité Berlin University Institute of Biochemistry.

items.title: 'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer
items.desc: Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach used to treat water that flows from the distant Liberty Reservoir into the facility, killing bacteria and other pathogens before it's routed to the region's kitchen sinks.

items.title: A fish as old as Montana—the blue sucker discovered to live well over 100 years
items.desc: Using bomb radiocarbon dating on microscopic otoliths (earstones), researchers have found that a native species of fish in the Upper Missouri River in Montana is living up to 130 years—more than triple the previous estimate of around 40 years—and some blue suckers alive today hatched in the late 1800s, around the dawn of the automobile and when Montana officially became a state.

items.title: Caribbean corals are in crisis. Fossil reefs can help point to where corals may persist
items.desc: The fossilized remains of ancient coral reefs often sit just meters from living corals in the Caribbean, where reefs have declined sharply over the past 70 years. Those fossils could help show where corals might survive a warming future. In two new papers, researchers at The University of Texas at Austin identify which coral species dominated ancient reefs in northeastern Jamaica and suggest how that record could guide reef rehabilitation.

items.title: Ancient bison hunting site in Texas challenges long-held assumptions
items.desc: For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Native American communities in the Southern Plains hunted bison by driving herds over cliffs, a sophisticated technique widely documented farther north.

items.title: Scientists discover twist-tunable interlayer excitons in atomically thin anisotropic semiconductors
items.desc: When light shines on a semiconductor, negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes—empty states left behind when electrons move away—pair up and bind together. This bound state is called an exciton. When two atomically thin semiconductor layers are stacked, electrons and holes can reside in different layers, forming what is known as an interlayer exciton (IE).

items.title: Gamified mobile payment features may drive adoption among Gen-Z users
items.desc: Gamified features in mobile payment applications may significantly increase adoption among consumers in emerging economies, with men and women responding in almost identical ways, according to research published in the International Journal of Business Information Systems.

items.title: Record-setting X-ray laser reliably generates flashes with wavelengths shorter than distances between atoms
items.desc: Researchers from DESY and European XFEL have demonstrated reliable production and transport of X-ray laser flashes with a wavelength of about 0.04 nanometers (or a photon energy of 30,000 electronvolts) at European XFEL, raising their own world record. This means that the X-ray's wavelength is much shorter than typical distances between neighboring atoms in solids, which enables the study of materials with higher spatial resolution than before.

items.title: Digital imaging workshop aims to reveal secrets in medieval manuscripts
items.desc: Researchers recently used multispectral imaging technology to try to uncover hidden information from medieval manuscripts at the Rare Book and Manuscript Library at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The library hosted a digital imaging workshop in early October that served as a pilot study for how the technology can help analyze fragile, centuries-old documents.

items.title: New hemp plant produces no detectable THC, potentially reducing risk of crop destruction
items.desc: Scientists at Texas A&M AgriLife Research, a member of The Texas A&M University System, have developed a hemp plant that produces no detectable cannabinoids, including THC.

items.title: Tested on mushrooms, an AI model shows potential for detecting crop stress with far fewer computations
items.desc: A new artificial intelligence (AI) model can detect stress in agricultural crops using a nondestructive imaging technique, allowing changes in crop health to be monitored over time. Developed by a team of researchers at Penn State, the new model shows promise for accurately detecting crop stress caused by drought, disease, nutrient deficiency and other causes while using less computing power than some existing AI methods.

items.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
items.desc: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

items.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
items.desc: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

items.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
items.desc: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.

items.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
items.desc: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

items.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
items.desc: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

items.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
items.desc: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.desc: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

items.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
items.desc: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.

items.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
items.desc: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.

items.title: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
items.desc: New research reveals that the brain makes free choices and forced decisions using surprisingly similar neural processes, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The discovery challenges assumptions about free will while suggesting that our personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.

items.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
items.desc: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.

items.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.desc: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

items.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
items.desc: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

items.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
items.desc: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.

items.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
items.desc: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.

items.title: Journalism Can Be More Than AI Fodder
items.desc: As AI fundamentally alters the information environment, news publishers risk becoming little more than content suppliers for Big Tech. To avoid that fate, many are drawing on their archives and expertise to develop AI tools that allow them to operate and compete on their own terms.

items.title: Governing African Economies as They Are
items.desc: Africa cannot overcome its development challenges by applying the same knowledge, economic, and innovation systems that helped create them. Imagining and governing new ways forward will require three intellectual ruptures.

items.title: Making Earth Cool Again
items.desc: Climate multilateralism is evolving into a two-tiered system in which high-level negotiations toward shared commitments and the real-world implementation of climate solutions become more mutually supportive. Only by unleashing such virtuous cycles can we keep the 1.5ºC target for global warming within reach.

items.title: America’s Lame-Duck Autocrat
items.desc: When autocrats suffer a defeat, they tend to double down, such as by intensifying repression at home or behaving more recklessly abroad. With two years left in office after historic midterm election losses, this is the road US President Donald Trump appears to be taking.

items.title: Getting Ukraine’s House in Order
items.desc: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly opposed the idea of forming a national unity government. But bringing opposition leaders into the cabinet would ensure the checks on corruption and wayward bureaucratic action that Zelensky’s team can no longer provide.

items.title: What Adam Smith Missed
items.desc: For all that he got right, the "founding father" of economics failed to see how technological innovations lead to market monopolization. If AI is left to the invisible hand, it will almost certainly increase economic and political inequality, causing even deeper social polarization and further undermining democracy.

items.title: China Ratchets Up Its Weaponization of Trade
items.desc: Just as the US has been leveraging its large market and technological leadership for geopolitical ends, China is now using its dominance in critical minerals, industrial inputs, and specialized manufacturing machinery to coerce and punish other countries. The consequences, both economic and geopolitical, are far-reaching.

items.title: There Is Only One Thing to Talk About With Russia
items.desc: The European security order’s foundational principle is never to tolerate aggression. There is no need to revise that order, as the Kremlin has proposed, only to wait for a Russian regime that is willing to respect other countries’ territorial integrity and uphold its own previous commitments.

items.title: The Truth About Global AI Governance
items.desc: Because the current approach to global AI governance presumes that developing countries are full of eager adopters of AI who need to be cautioned about the technology's risks, it overlooks what their information environments and media markets actually need. A survey of researchers who study 71 countries sets the record straight.

items.title: Demography is the Achilles’ Heel of Dictatorships
items.desc: Governments that manipulate population figures often end up deceiving themselves as much as the public. When autocratic leaders mistake inflated numbers for real national strength, they make costly strategic mistakes and fail to address their countries’ demographic decline until it is too late.

items.title: The Silver Lining of a Data-Center Slowdown
items.desc: With leading AI labs under intense competitive pressure to keep advancing the frontier of the technology's capabilities, resistance to the build-out of computing resources is not such a bad thing. The more time we can buy, the greater our chances of maximizing the potential benefits and mitigating the risks.

items.title: What Nvidia’s Crisis Reveals About the Chip War
items.desc: Export restrictions, like those depriving China of Nvidia’s most advanced chips, may buy time by curtailing a competitor's access to frontier capabilities made elsewhere. But in any technological conflict, policymakers must remember that slowing a rival is not the same as strengthening oneself.

items.title: When Export Restraints Are the Lesser Evil
items.desc: Governments face pressure to protect domestic industries while preserving access to cheaper foreign goods. The recent EU-China car-export deal offers an uneasy compromise that protects European automakers while keeping Chinese cars available to consumers, making it preferable to prohibitive tariffs.

items.title: The Trade Losses That Nobody Counts
items.desc: While much of the United Kingdom’s post-Brexit debate has focused on the monetary value of lost trade with the European Union, the composition of UK-EU trade flows warrants closer attention. A sharp decline in the variety of products shipped to Europe suggests that the economic costs have been greater than many realize.

items.title: Nigeria’s Big Bet on Health Care
items.desc: Nigeria’s dependence on imported medicines and medical equipment leaves families exposed to exchange-rate fluctuations and hospitals at the mercy of global supply chains. Expanding domestic manufacturing is essential to reducing the cost of treatment and ensuring that more Nigerians can access quality care.

items.desc: Policymakers have recently proposed requiring “AI kill switches” to quickly stop an AI system or limit the impact of a harmful or unwanted AI incident.
